title: ArrayDeque vs LinkedList vs Stack: when to use each
shortTitle: When do you use ArrayDeque vs LinkedList vs Stack?
keyPoints: ArrayDeque is the fastest general-purpose Deque, Stack, and Queue implementation; it is backed by a resizable circular array with O(1) amortized operations at both ends
ArrayDeque beats LinkedList for Deque operations because contiguous memory gives excellent CPU cache locality
ArrayDeque beats Stack because Stack extends Vector, which synchronizes every method even in single-threaded code
ArrayDeque does not allow null elements because null is used internally as an empty sentinel
ArrayDeque does not implement List, so it has no get(index) or set(index) methods
LinkedList is appropriate only when you need both List and Deque interfaces on the same object or need to store null elements
Never use Stack in new code; the Javadoc itself recommends ArrayDeque as the replacement

s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayDeque is the fastest Deque/Stack/Queue implementation in Java, backed by a circular array with O(1) operations at both ends, beating LinkedList in speed and Stack in design.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **ArrayDeque** is a resizable circular array implementing `Deque`; it provides O(1) amortized add/remove at both ends with excellent cache locality
- **LinkedList** implements both `List` and `Deque` but uses scattered heap nodes, causing cache misses that make it 2-3x slower than ArrayDeque for deque operations
- **Stack** extends `Vector` (Java 1.0), synchronizing every method; it also exposes `get(index)` which violates the LIFO abstraction
- The Java documentation states: "This class is likely to be faster than Stack when used as a stack, and faster than LinkedList when used as a queue"
s1_definition.analogy: ArrayDeque is a modern bank counter with two service windows – one at each end – fast service, no unnecessary paperwork. LinkedList as a Deque is like passing sticky notes through a chain of people, each note scattered in a different room. Stack is an old counter with a heavy lock on the door – even one customer must wait for the lock to open and close.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ArrayDeque circular array

  elements[]: [_, _, C, D, E, F, _, _]
                    ↑              ↑
                   head           tail

  addFirst(B):  [_, B, C, D, E, F, _, _]
                 ↑
                head (moved left)

  addLast(G):   [_, B, C, D, E, F, G, _]
                                      ↑
                                     tail (moved right)

  pollFirst():  [_, _, C, D, E, F, G, _]  returns B
                    ↑
                   head (moved right)

  Wrapping:
  elements[]: [H, _, _, _, _, F, G, _]
               ↑                 ↑
              tail              head
  Head at index 5, tail at index 1 – circular!

  Decision:
  Queue (FIFO)  → ArrayDeque
  Stack (LIFO)  → ArrayDeque
  List + Deque  → LinkedList
  Thread-safe   → ConcurrentLinkedDeque
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayDeque is the modern, fast replacement for both the legacy Stack class and LinkedList when used as a queue or deque. It is backed by a resizable circular array that provides O(1) amortized operations at both ends with excellent CPU cache locality. It uses about 10x less memory per element than LinkedList and avoids the synchronization overhead of Stack.

In the National Bank of India's transaction processing system, Rajesh uses ArrayDeque for the transaction processing queue. Incoming transactions are added to the tail with `offerLast()`, and the processing thread removes them from the head with `pollFirst()`. For the undo stack in the account management UI, he uses the same ArrayDeque with `push()` and `pop()`. Both patterns are faster and lighter than the alternatives.

LinkedList as a Deque is appropriate only when you also need the List interface (get by index, though it is O(n)) or when you need to store null elements. Stack should never be used in new code – its own Javadoc recommends ArrayDeque.

Remember one sentence: ArrayDeque is the default choice for queue, stack, and deque – it is faster than LinkedList, lighter than Stack, and backed by a cache-friendly circular array.
